title: The teacher’s prayer: for understanding, for means, and for students
theme: A teacher asks Om — ‘the bull of the Vedas’ — first for intelligence and a body fit to learn, then for prosperity, then for students who will come as water runs downhill.

translation.literal: Who, the bull of the Vedic hymns, having every form, arose out of the hymns, out of the immortal — may he, Indra, strengthen me with intelligence. O god, may I be a bearer of the immortal. My body [be] able; my tongue most full of sweetness; with the ears may I hear much. You are the sheath of Brahman, covered by intelligence; guard my learning. Bringing, spreading out,
translation.readable: May the one who is chief of the Vedic hymns, who takes every form, who arose from the immortal hymns — may that lord strengthen me with understanding. O god, may I hold what leads to immortality. May my body be able, my tongue speak sweetly, my ears hear much. You are the sheath in which Brahman is kept, hidden by ordinary understanding: guard what I have learned. Bringing and increasing,

morphology.note: Nominative plural used where the construction wants an accusative (‘making clothes and cows’). Kūranārāyaṇa calls it a Vedic exchange of cases: «विभक्तिव्यत्ययश्छान्दसः».
The base file writes वासां सि with a space inside the word, as it did with सं हिता; the letters are those of vāsāṃsi.
Imperative of vah with ā, ‘bring’. Śaṅkara and Gopālānanda take the one addressed to be the same as in the first unit: Om («अधिकारादोङ्कार एवाभिसम्बध्यते»).
Imperative of i, ‘go’; with ā, ‘come’; with vi and pra, ‘come from different places’, ‘come forth’.

The division of damāyantu and śamāyantu is not explained by Śaṅkara or Kūranārāyaṇa. The comment printed after Kūranārāyaṇa’s in the six-commentary file takes dam and śam as words qualifying the students; the division followed here is its reading, and is uncertain.

translation.literal: making quickly for myself clothes and cows, and food and drink always — [that prosperity] then bring to me, prosperity with wool, together with cattle. Svāhā. May students come to me. Svāhā. May students come to me from all sides. Svāhā. May students come forth to me. Svāhā. May self-restrained students come. Svāhā. May calm students come. Svāhā.
translation.readable: and quickly providing me with clothes and cattle, food and drink at all times — bring me, after that, such prosperity, rich in sheep and other animals. Svāhā. May students come to me; may they come from everywhere; may they come forward; may they come restrained; may they come at peace. Svāhā.

samasa.meaning: in the one who has a thousand branches
that which wears away the days: the year

morphology.note: Imperative first person singular of as, ‘to be’: ‘let me be’. The first-person imperative ends in āni (P. 3.4.92 (आडुत्तमस्य पिच्च) adds the augment ā).
A Vedic comparative of vasu, ‘good, rich’, equivalent to vasīyas (Kūranārāyaṇa: «छन्दसः ईकारलोपः»), here ablative of comparison: ‘better than the richer’.
The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha inserts t before s (तस्मिन्त्सहस्रशाखे), an optional junction of recitation (corrections.json).
Present middle of mṛj, ‘wipe, cleanse’, with the preverb ni standing apart: ni … mṛje, ‘I wipe myself clean’.

Vocative of dhātṛ, ‘arranger, ordainer’. Its pausal form is dhātaḥ; it is written here as it stands before the vowel of āyantu, because its visarga goes back to r (the sandhi checker’s list of r-final words does not include it). Madhva’s text reads dhātar ā yantu brahmacāriṇaḥ (corrections.json).

Imperative of bhā, ‘shine’, with pra separated: pra … bhāhi. The base file printed pāhi, ‘protect’; the edition reads bhāhi with Śaṅkara’s gloss, the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text (corrections.json). Kūranārāyaṇa also reads bhāhi and takes it causatively, ‘make me shine’: «प्रभाहीति अन्तर्भावितण्यर्थः».

translation.literal: May I be renowned among people. Svāhā. May I be better than the richer. Svāhā. Into you, such as you are, O Bhaga, may I enter. Svāhā. You, O Bhaga, enter me. Svāhā. In you, thousand-branched, O Bhaga, I wipe myself clean. Svāhā. As waters go by a slope, as months [go] to the year, so, O Dhātṛ, may students come to me from every side. Svāhā. You are a resting-place; shine forth to me, come forth to me.
translation.readable: May I be known among people. Svāhā. May I be better than the wealthy. Svāhā. May I enter you, gracious one. Svāhā. Gracious one, enter me. Svāhā. In you, the one with a thousand branches, I wash myself clean. Svāhā. As water runs downhill, as the months run into the year, so may students come to me from every side, Ordainer. Svāhā. You are a shelter close at hand: shine on me; come to me.

syntax: Unit 1 opens with a relative clause (‘who … arose’) resumed by ‘he’ (sa) and a third-person imperative (spṛṇotu). Then come first-person wishes in the benedictive and verbless wishes (‘my body [be] able’), a second-person statement (‘you are the sheath of Brahman’) and an imperative (‘guard’). From āvahantī a long feminine participial phrase describes an unnamed ‘she’ who brings and increases, resolved only at ‘bring me prosperity (śriyam)’. Units 2–3 are short formulas each closed by svāhā, mostly imperatives in the first and third person; the preverbs ā, vi, pra, ni and pra are several times separated from their verbs. Two comparisons with yathā … evam close the prayer for students.

ambiguities.note: The text names ‘the bull of the hymns, having every form’, ‘Indra’, ‘god’, ‘Bhaga’, ‘Dhātṛ’, but never says Om. Śaṅkara: Om, the object of meditation here («ओङ्कारो ह्यत्रोपास्य इति»), praised with the names of the lord. Kūranārāyaṇa: the praṇava as that which expresses the supreme Brahman («अत्र परब्रह्मवाचकः प्रणवः विद्यागन्त्वेन स्तूयते»), and in the later formulas the Lord of Śrī himself. Madhva: Hari (see the Dvaita position).

‘You are the sheath of Brahman, covered by medhā’. Śaṅkara: Om is where Brahman is perceived, as a sword in its scabbard, but it is hidden by worldly understanding. Kūranārāyaṇa: all the Vedas and Brahman lie in it like treasure in a jewel-casket, and it is ‘covered by medhā’ in the sense of divine knowledge, so that those without it cannot grasp it («ज्ञानविशेषदर्शनीयस्वरूपत्वात् तज्ज्ञानरहितानां दुर्ग्रहोऽसीति»). The same word medhā is the gift asked for at the start of the anuvāka.
kurvāṇācīram can be divided kurvāṇā acīram, ‘making quickly’, or kurvāṇā cīram, ‘making for long’. Śaṅkara gives both, preferring the first; Kūranārāyaṇa also gives both.

Kūranārāyaṇa first takes yaśaḥ as ‘renowned’ (the sense of a possessive suffix understood) and jane as ‘among people’; he and Śaṅkara also read yaśojane as a compound, ‘among the renowned’ («यशोजने यशस्विजनेषु»). The padaccheda follows the first reading.
The last two student formulas are not explained by Śaṅkara (‘and so on’). The division dam / śam + āyantu follows the comment printed after Kūranārāyaṇa’s in the six-commentary file; it is uncertain.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Metrical and prose formulas mixed. Unit 1’s lines count 11, 10, 9, 12, 8, 8, 8, 12, 6 and 8 syllables: Kūranārāyaṇa calls the opening a madhyejyotis triṣṭubh («मध्येज्योतिस्त्रिष्टुप्») followed by a three-footed gāyatrī («त्रिपदा गायत्री»), the rest yajus. In the homa formulas he counts a six-footed jagatī from āvahantī («आवहन्तीति प्रथमा षट्पदा जगती»: lines of 8 with 10 in the sixth, svāhā included) and a five-footed second verse («द्वितीया पञ्चपदा»); the five student formulas have 11 syllables each. His analysis is reported, not tested; the syllable counts are irregular for every standard metre.

beginner: This is a teacher’s prayer, and it asks for things in a careful order. First: a mind that understands and remembers, a healthy body, a kind tongue, ears that hear a great deal, and protection for what has already been learned. Only then does it ask for wealth — clothes, cattle, food — because, as a commentator says, money in the hands of someone without judgement only does harm. Then it asks for students: that they come, self-controlled and calm, from every direction, as naturally as water runs downhill. It also asks to be good, to be respected, and to be washed clean. The one addressed is, for the commentators, the sacred syllable Om, through which the highest reality is approached.
analogy: Like someone setting up a school who first asks for a clear head, then for the money to keep the doors open, and then for pupils — in that order, because the building is worthless without the teacher’s understanding, and the understanding is lonely without the pupils.

commentary.q: What does the passage actually say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It addresses one who is ‘bull of the hymns, having every form’, arisen from the immortal hymns, and asks him to strengthen the speaker with medhā; asks to be a bearer of the immortal, with an able body, a sweet tongue and ears that hear much; calls him ‘the sheath of Brahman, covered by medhā’ and asks him to guard what has been learned. Then it asks for prosperity that provides clothes, cattle, food and drink, and for students, in formulas ending in svāhā; for renown, for excellence, for mutual ‘entering’ with Bhaga, for cleansing in the ‘thousand-branched’; and that students come like water down a slope and months into the year. It ends: ‘you are a resting-place; shine forth to me, come to me’. The name Om does not occur.

commentary.q: Why is a prayer for wealth inside an Upaniṣad?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara classifies the anuvāka as mantras of recitation and oblation for one who desires intelligence and one who desires prosperity: «मेधाकामस्य श्रीकामस्य च तत्प्राप्तिसाधनं जपहोमावुच्येते». He justifies the prayer for wealth in a teaching about knowledge by a chain of means: «श्रीकामोऽस्मिन्विद्याप्रकरणे अभिधीयमानो धनार्थः», wealth is for ritual action, «कर्म च उपात्तदुरितक्षयार्थम्», and «तत्क्षये हि विद्या प्रकाशते» — when past wrongdoing is exhausted, knowledge shines. He explains why wealth comes after intelligence (tataḥ, ‘then’): «अमेधसो हि श्रीरनर्थायैवेति» — for one without intelligence, prosperity only does harm. Gopālānanda (modern) spells out the same chain: without wealth no rites, without rites no purification, without a clear mind no knowledge.

commentary.q: Who is ‘the bull of the hymns’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: Om, chief of the Vedas and ‘having every form’ because it pervades all speech, as the Chāndogya says (parallels): «ओङ्कारो ह्यत्रोपास्य इति ऋषभादिशब्दैः स्तुतिर्न्याय्यैव ओङ्कारस्य». ‘Arose from the immortal hymns’ cannot mean that the eternal Om was produced; it means Om shone forth to Prajāpati as their essence — «न हि नित्यस्य ओङ्कारस्य अञ्जसैवोत्पत्तिरवकल्पते». Kūranārāyaṇa also takes it as the praṇava, and sees in the praise a likeness between the praṇava, Brahman as word, and Nārāyaṇa, Brahman as reality: «साधर्म्यं प्रतिपाद्यते».

commentary.q: What is asked for first, and why the body?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara takes medhā as strength of understanding («प्रज्ञाबलं हि प्रार्थ्यते») and ‘bearer of the immortal’ as holding the knowledge of Brahman. The requests for an able body, a sweet tongue and ears that hear much amount to one wish: «आत्मज्ञानयोग्यः कार्यकरणसङ्घातोऽस्त्विति वाक्यार्थः» — may this complex of body and senses be fit for knowledge of the Self.

commentary.q: ‘May I enter you; enter me’ — union or service?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads the exchange as identity: having entered you, may I become you and nothing else, «प्रविश्य चानन्यस्त्वदात्मैव भवानीत्यर्थः», «आवयोरेकात्मत्वमेवास्तु»; and ‘come to me’ as ‘make me one with you, like iron steeped in mercury’, «रसविद्धमिव लोहं त्वन्मयं त्वदात्मानं कुर्वित्यर्थः». Kūranārāyaṇa addresses Bhaga as the Lord of Śrī and reads ‘entering’ as reaching him as one who enjoys him, receiving the whole of service to him — «भोक्तृत्वेन प्राप्नुवानि», «अशेषं कैङ्कर्यं लभेय» — and ‘enter me’ as a plea to be accepted, as the sages of the Daṇḍaka forest were: «दण्डकारण्यवासिनः शरभङ्गादिमुनिवर्यानिव त्वमेव मां स्वीकुरु». The same words carry the two schools’ different ends: becoming one, or being taken into service.

commentary.q: pāhi or bhāhi in the last line?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base file (Śaṅkara’s mūla in Advaita Sharada) prints ‘pra mā pāhi’, ‘protect me’; the edition reads bhāhi, ‘shine’, because Śaṅkara’s own gloss explains bhāhi («मा मां प्रति प्रभाहि प्रकाशयात्मानम्») and the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text agree (corrections.json). Kūranārāyaṇa also reads bhāhi («प्रभाहीति अन्तर्भावितण्यर्थः»). But pāhi has commentarial support too: Gopālānanda writes «मां प्र पाहि», and the comment printed after Kūranārāyaṇa’s explains «प्रपाहि मां प्ररक्ष». The reading is not settled by the commentaries alone.

advaita.text: For Śaṅkara the addressee is Om as the symbol in which Brahman is perceived («त्वं हि ब्रह्मणः प्रतीकम् , त्वयि ब्रह्मोपलभ्यते»). The prayers for intelligence serve knowledge of the Self; the prayers for wealth serve it indirectly, through rites that remove the wrongdoing that obscures knowledge, and he cites a smṛti to that effect. The mutual ‘entering’ is read as identity with that which Om stands for.

visistadvaita.text: Kūranārāyaṇa reads the praṇava as the word that expresses the supreme Brahman, praised as a limb of the knowledge («अत्र परब्रह्मवाचकः प्रणवः विद्यागन्त्वेन स्तूयते»), and the later formulas as addressed to the Lord with Śrī. ‘Entering’ is attainment as one who enjoys the Lord, completed in service (kaiṅkarya), and ‘enter me’ asks the Lord to accept the devotee. The ‘sheath of Brahman’ is a jewel-casket in which the Vedas and the Lord with his qualities are kept («रत्नमञ्जूशिकायां निधिरिव निहितमिति»).

dvaita.text: Madhva’s comment consists of verses he cites (without naming their source beyond ‘इति प्रक्लृप्ते’ and ‘इति च’). They make Hari the subject throughout: the bull of the hymns is «यो विश्वरूपो भगवांश्च्छन्दसामधिपो हरिः»; he is ‘the sheath of Brahman’ because the Vedas dwell in him, «वेदावासत्वतो विष्णुर्ब्रह्मकोश इति स्मृतः»; Bhaga because he is full of the six qualities, «भगः षड्गुणपूर्णत्वाद्»; and, pervading all, ‘thousand-branched’ because he has many forms («बहुरूपत्वतो विभुः»). These verses are reported as cited by Madhva, not as verified quotations of any work.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara and Kūranārāyaṇa both make Om the addressee of the opening and read the praise as of what Om expresses; Madhva makes Hari the addressee directly. On ‘may I enter you, enter me’ the schools divide sharply: identity (Śaṅkara), attainment and service (Kūranārāyaṇa). All agree that the prayers for wealth and students serve the life of learning.

parallels.note: Śaṅkara cites this passage to explain why Om is ‘having every form’ (viśvarūpa): all speech is held together by Om as leaves on a stalk.
The Kaṭha calls the syllable Om Brahman and the highest. A thematic association with Om as ‘the sheath of Brahman’.

parallels.quote: प्रणवो धनुः शरो ह्यात्मा ब्रह्म तल्लक्ष्यमुच्यते
parallels.note: In the Muṇḍaka Om is the bow by which the self reaches Brahman. Like this anuvāka it treats Om as the means of approach, not the goal itself.

contemporary.text: The prayer does not despise money: it asks for clothes, food and cattle without embarrassment. But it asks for them second, after a clear mind and a body fit to learn, and Śaṅkara gives the reason bluntly — prosperity in the hands of someone without judgement only does harm. Many people today seek resources first and hope wisdom will follow. The order here suggests the reverse, and treats wealth as something that serves learning and teaching rather than the measure of a life. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you could ask for three things for your studies, in order, what would they be?
reflect.deeper: Why might a teacher pray for students, and what does that say about how knowledge is kept alive?
reflect.practice: Before your next purchase, ask whether it serves something you are learning or making. Notice how often the answer changes the decision.

references.text: Śaṅkara closes with a smṛti verse, «ज्ञानमुत्पद्यते पुंसां क्षयात्पापस्य कर्मणः», with the editor’s references to the Mahābhārata (Śānti) and the Garuḍa Purāṇa; Kūranārāyaṇa repeats it. Reported as cited by them; not verified in those works here.

Kūranārāyaṇa’s comment in the six-commentary file is followed, without a new attribution line, by a second comment on this anuvāka marked ‘आ.भा.’; this edition quotes it only as ‘the comment printed after Kūranārāyaṇa’s’.

flags.note: pāhi / bhāhi in the last line: corrected to bhāhi on the evidence of Śaṅkara’s gloss, the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text, but Gopālānanda and the ‘आ.भा.’ comment read pāhi. The correction should be reviewed against a printed Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.
Madhva’s text reads dhātar ā yantu brahmacāriṇaḥ for dhātar āyantu sarvataḥ; the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha writes tasmint sahasraśākhe (corrections.json).
The division of damāyantu / śamāyantu as dam āyantu / śam āyantu follows a single, imperfectly attributed comment.

The padaccheda writes the vocative dhātar in its pre-vocalic form rather than the pausal dhātaḥ, because the sandhi checker does not list dhātaḥ among r-final words. If dhātaḥ is added to that list, the padaccheda should be changed to धातः.

The second comment on this anuvāka inside the Kūranārāyaṇa witness file (marked ‘आ.भा.’) may belong to another commentator in the six-commentary edition; its attribution needs checking against the printed book.
